candidate.answerReason: Representing the regular and large drinks as 2 and 3 equal parts shows that the extra 2 ounces equal one-quarter of a part. Each part is 8 ounces, and the combined 5 parts total 40 ounces.

methods.label: Use equal parts to track the transfer
methods.explanation:
Call the regular drink 2 equal parts. Since the large drink is \(50\%\) larger, it contains 3 of these parts. Together the drinks contain 5 parts.

They finish all the lemonade and drink equal amounts, so each person consumes \(\tfrac52\) parts. Ed started with 2 parts and receives lemonade only from Ann. Therefore Ann must transfer
\[
\frac52-2=\frac12
\]
of a part to Ed.

After Ann consumes \(\tfrac34\) of her drink, she has \(\tfrac14\cdot3=\tfrac34\) of a part left. One-third of that remainder is
\[
\frac13\cdot\frac34=\frac14
\]
of a part. The additional 2 ounces must make up the rest of the required transfer, namely
\[
\frac12-\frac14=\frac14
\]
of a part. Thus one whole part is \(2\div\tfrac14=8\) ounces, and the combined amount is \(5\cdot8=40\) ounces.

These sizes are feasible: the drinks start at 16 and 24 ounces. Ann has 6 ounces left when she transfers \(6/3+2=4\) ounces, making each person's total consumption 20 ounces. Together they drink \(\boxed{40}\) ounces, choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

review.mathematicalCheck: With initial amounts of 2 and 3 parts, equal final consumption requires a transfer of half a part. The prescribed fractional transfer contributes one-quarter of a part, so 2 ounces equal the remaining quarter-part. Each part is 8 ounces and the total is 40. The numerical check verifies that Ann has enough lemonade to make the transfer.
